problem.text: Lily pads $1, 2, 3, \ldots$ lie in a row on a pond. A frog makes a sequence of jumps starting on pad $1$. From any pad $k$ the frog jumps to either pad $k+1$ or pad $k+2$ chosen randomly with probability $\frac{1}{2}$ and independently of other jumps. The probability that the frog visits pad $7$ is $\frac{p}{q}$, where $p$ and $q$ are relatively prime positive integers. Find $p+q$.

steps.title: Where to start: ask how the frog can land on a pad
steps.body: The frog only moves forward by $1$ or $2$, so it can land on pad $n$ only by jumping from pad $n - 1$ or from pad $n - 2$. That suggests building the answer pad by pad. Let $p_n$ be the probability that the frog ever visits pad $n$. The frog starts on pad $1$, so $p_1 = 1$.

your_turn.answer: $p_2 = \frac{1}{2}$: the only way to visit pad $2$ is for the very first jump to be $+1$.

steps.title: Write the rule for $p_n$
steps.body:
For $n \ge 3$, the frog visits pad $n$ exactly when it visits pad $n-1$ and then jumps $+1$, or visits pad $n-2$ and then jumps $+2$. These two ways cannot both happen, because a $+2$ jump from pad $n-2$ skips pad $n-1$. So we can add them:
$$p_n = \tfrac{1}{2}p_{n-1} + \tfrac{1}{2}p_{n-2}$$

steps.title: Keep going up the row
steps.body: Each new value is the average of the two before it. Careful: these probabilities do not add up to $1$, since the frog visits many pads, so do not try to normalize them. Just keep averaging.

steps.title: Put it together
steps.body:
Two more averages give $p_6 = \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{11}{16} + \frac{5}{8}\right) = \frac{21}{32}$ and
$$p_7 = \tfrac{1}{2}\left(\tfrac{21}{32} + \tfrac{11}{16}\right) = \tfrac{43}{64}.$$
Since $43$ is odd, the fraction is in lowest terms, so $p + q = 43 + 64 = 107$. The answer is **$107$**.
